from_notes: Freedom from arrest: only in civil cases ... during session and 40 days before and after
x: Freedom from arrest applies only in civil cases and only during a session and 40 days before and after it, not 'whether Parliament is in session or not'. Free speech (Art. 105(1)), the right to publish proceedings and the rule that no member is arrested within the precincts without the presiding officer's permission are all correct.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.378 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity APPSC 21 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-21.txt)

x: The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction covers constitutional (Art. 132), civil (Art. 133) and criminal (Art. 134) cases. Disputes arising out of pre-Constitution treaties and agreements are excluded from its original jurisdiction (Art. 131 proviso), so that option is the one not involved.

from_notes: Punishments: admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, suspension/expulsion
x: A House punishes members and outsiders by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion (Raja Ram Pal 2007 upheld expulsion). It does not impose fines, and imprisonment lasts only till the session ends, so 'six months' is wrong.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.378 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Punishments: admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, suspension/expulsion
x: A House punishes by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion. It does not impose fines, and imprisonment cannot outlast the session, so expulsion with the seat declared vacant is the valid option.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.378 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Freedom from arrest: only in civil cases, not criminal or preventive detention
x: Members cannot be arrested during a session and 40 days before and after it, but only in civil cases, not criminal or preventive detention cases. Privileges are both collective and individual, outsiders can be punished too, and contempt is wider than breach of privilege.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.378 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Members' individual privileges include freedom of speech, freedom from arrest in civil cases and freedom from attendance as a witness while the House sits. Privileges are also collective (of each House), so 'only individual freedom' is the incorrect statement.

from_notes: 122 / 212 | Courts cannot question proceedings for procedural irregularity

from_notes: 105 / 194 | Privileges, freedom of speech, immunity

source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Prime Minister (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Constitution Art. 75(1)

x: The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha (majority party rule); the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: The President is not the real head of the executive (APPSC G2 2017).
x: The President is only the nominal (de jure) head; the real executive is the PM and Council of Ministers. The other statements correctly describe collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha, ministers holding office at the President's pleasure and tenure depending on the legislature.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Under Art. 75(3) the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, not to both Houses, the President or the ruling party.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: A is false: collective responsibility is only to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)). R is true: members of either House can be ministers.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: 1 and 2 are implied: ministers are members of Parliament (double membership) and hold office while they enjoy its confidence. 3 is wrong: the Cabinet is headed by the PM (head of government), not the Head of State.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: In a parliamentary system the government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it through a no-confidence vote.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Art. 75(3): the Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Under the parliamentary form, real executive power is exercised by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers; the President is the nominal head.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: The Council of Ministers is responsible to the legislature – strictly the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)); among the options, Parliament. Individual responsibility to the President is a different matter.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Cabinet membership is not restricted to Lok Sabha members: ministers may come from either House, and a non-member may be a minister for six months (Art. 75(5)).
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: In a presidential government all executive power is vested in the President, who is both head of State and head of government.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Leadership of the PM: ... Leader of the Lok Sabha
x: By convention the Prime Minister is the Leader of the Lok Sabha if he is its member (otherwise he names a minister, e.g. Pranab Mukherjee under Manmohan Singh).
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Art. 75(5): a minister who is not a member of either House for six consecutive months ceases to be a minister.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct (double membership; office while enjoying confidence). 3 is wrong: the Cabinet is headed by the Prime Minister, not the Head of State.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: A is false: collective responsibility is to the Lok Sabha only (Art. 75(3)). R is true: members of both Houses can be ministers.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: A and R both true, R explains A (UPPSC 2025)
x: Both are true and R explains A: India is parliamentary because the executive is responsible to the legislature (Art. 75(3), Art. 164(2)).
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Only B is correct: revenue bills must originate in the US House of Representatives (Art. I, s.7). A is wrong – the US Constitution came into force in 1789. C is wrong – John Quincy Adams, son of John Adams, was also a President's son.
source: US Constitution Art. I s.7 and National Archives (archives.gov); White House – Presidents (whitehouse.gov)

from_notes: APPSC G2 2025 key: head of State, head of Government, directly elected = correct; accountable to the legislature = wrong
x: The US-type President is head of State and head of government and is (in effect) directly elected, but is not accountable to the legislature, so i, ii and iii.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: In a presidential system the President heads the executive, appoints his own secretaries (cabinet) and cannot dissolve the legislature – all three are features.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: A single executive (the President is both head of State and of government) is the basic feature of presidential government.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Presidential government rests on separation of powers with checks and balances – the President and the legislature check each other (veto, Senate confirmation, impeachment). Fusion of powers is parliamentary; 'division of powers' describes federalism.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
evidence: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: The presidential form was first formed in the USA (1787 Constitution), its oldest and purest form.
source: Rocket Polity Sheets p.3 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Supremacy | Constitutional supremacy (written Constitution) | Sovereignty of Parliament
x: Sovereignty of Parliament is a British feature; India has constitutional supremacy with judicial review. The other three are features of the Indian Constitution.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Judicial review | Courts can strike down laws; basic structure | Courts cannot question Acts of Parliament
x: India, unlike Britain, has judicial review – courts can strike down laws. A real and nominal executive, collective responsibility and bicameralism exist in both.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Art. 315(2): two or more States may agree to have a Joint State Public Service Commission, created by an Act of Parliament on the request of their legislatures.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. State Public Service Commission – JSPSC (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02.txt)

x: Pawan Kumar Chamling (Sikkim, 1994-2019, about 24 years 5 months) holds the record as the longest-serving Chief Minister; Naveen Patnaik (2000-2024) ended just short of it, and Jyoti Basu served about 23 years.
source: Sikkim Legislative Assembly / news reports on Naveen Patnaik's tenure, June 2024 (pib.gov.in, thehindu.com)
evidence: The Hindu, June 2024 – Patnaik short of Chamling's record

add_option: The Executive is responsible to the Legislature
x: In a parliamentary form the executive is responsible to the legislature. None of the printed options says so: the legislature is not responsible to the judiciary or the executive, independence of legislature and executive is the presidential feature, and the President is not responsible to the judiciary.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
evidence: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Only the pocket veto is common: both the Indian and US Presidents have it. Residuary powers lie with the Union in India but with the States in the USA, and only India's upper house has nominated members.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Laxmikanth ch. President – Veto Power (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: The parliamentary system operates on the responsibility of the executive to the legislature.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

from_notes: Main advantage of parliamentary government: executive stays responsible to the legislature
x: The main advantage is that the executive stays responsible to the legislature (responsible government); continuity of policy is a presidential advantage and parliamentary governments can change without election.
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: The main advantage of the parliamentary form is that the executive remains responsible to the legislature (UPSC 2017 key).
source: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)

x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly (4 Nov 1948) that the parliamentary system gives a daily assessment of responsibility (questions, motions, debates) as well as a periodic one by the electorate, which he found more effective than the American periodic assessment.
source: Constituent Assembly Debates vol. 7, 4 Nov 1948 (eparlib.sansad.in); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.13 p.206-209 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
